title: Multilingual Code-Switching Architectures: Modeling Nigerian Pidgin-English Interfaces in Large Language Models
linguistic_thesis: The seamless code-switching between Nigerian Pidgin (Naija) and standard English within conversational data creates dynamic syntactic blends that confound rigid monolingual parsers. Effective NLP modeling requires specialized sub-tokenizers and mixed-code attention mechanisms.
technical_analysis: This report investigates the computational challenges of modeling fluid code-switching and code-mixing between Nigerian Pidgin (Naija) and Nigerian English within modern neural network architectures. In natural urban discourse across Lagos, Port Harcourt, and Ibadan, speakers constantly oscillate between acrolectal NigE, basilectal Pidgin, and indigenous substrate languages (such as Yorùbá, Ìgbò, and Hausa). Standard multilingual language models, while trained on massive web scrapes, severely underrepresent this mixed register, treating code-switched utterances as noisy or ungrammatical text. Syntactically, this contact phenomenon features complex restructuring, such as the copula deletion in Pidgin ('E good' vs. 'It is good') merging with English complement clauses ('She said that e good'). Tokenization bottlenecks are acute; standard byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizers fragment Pidgin particles like 'na', 'dey', and 'relegating' them into disjointed subword tokens that dilute semantic coherence. Historically, Nigerian Pidgin has evolved from a historical trade language into an autonomous, urban lingua franca imbued with high covert prestige and expansive expressive power. From an NLP standpoint, this necessitates the development of specialized adapter modules (such as LoRA weights tuned on mixed-corpus data) that preserve both the formal requirements of bureaucratic writing and the dynamic fluidity of digital Pidgin discourse. Our corpus analysis demonstrates that models augmented with dynamic language-identification layers achieve significantly lower perplexity scores on mixed Nigerian datasets, preventing catastrophic forgetting of standard English syntax while accurately parsing localized pragmatic markers.

title: Computational Detection of Sarcasm and Indirect Understatement in Nigerian English Conversational Mesolects
linguistic_thesis: Sentiment analysis models routinely misclassify Nigerian English understatement and hyper-polite sarcasm as literal compliance due to divergent illocutionary force indicators. The pragmatic layering of direct semantic praise over critical intent requires context-aware attention mechanisms trained on localized conversational data.
technical_analysis: Sarcasm and understatement in Nigerian English mesolectal and acrolectal interactions operate through specialized pragmatic markers that confound standard NLP sentiment classifiers. Unlike American English, where sarcasm is frequently cued by extreme prosodic exaggeration or explicit lexical markers, NigE irony often relies on deadpan delivery combined with hyper-formal praise formulae (e.g., 'Well done, professor of mathematics' uttered to someone who miscalculated basic change). Computational models trained on Western datasets evaluate the positive polarity words ('well done') and assign a positive sentiment score, completely missing the inverse illocutionary force. Furthermore, understatement in NigE ('It is not small work' meaning 'This is an overwhelming, nearly impossible task') employs litotes that are structurally inverted by binary sentiment scoring engines. Substrate influences from languages like Yoruba and Igbo contribute to this dynamic through tonal shifts and conventionalized rhetorical indirectness, where direct confrontation is avoided in favor of layered allegorical phrasing. In corpus linguistics, annotating such data requires multi-tier tagging that separates literal lexical polarity from pragmatic speech act intent. Failure to account for these nuances leads to severe algorithmic bias in automated content moderation, customer service sentiment tracking, and social media analytics across West African digital spaces. To resolve this, conversational datasets must incorporate turn-level pragmatic annotations that capture localized socio-cultural context, turn-taking dynamics, and shared background knowledge among speakers.

title: Curating Balanced Corpora for Nigerian English: Addressing Sub-Regional Variational Imbalances in NLP Training Sets
linguistic_thesis: The compilation of representative computational corpora for Nigerian English requires deliberate stratification across ethnolinguistic axes to mitigate baseline skews favoring Yoruba- and Igbo-influenced acrolects over Northern Hausa-English contact varieties. Neglecting these deep sociolinguistic topographies compromises the downstream perplexity scores of Large Language Models when applied to regional administrative discourse.
technical_analysis: Corpus compilation in post-colonial multilingual ecologies necessitates a departure from traditional Western sampling frames. Nigerian English (NigE) exists along a dynamic cline ranging from the basilectal Pidgin-infused register to the acrolectal standard utilized in parliamentary and academic institutions. In curating balanced corpora for NLP ingestion, engineers face severe data sparsity regarding Northern Nigerian Englishes, which are heavily influenced by Hausa substrate syntax, Islamate cultural frames, and distinct prosodic transfer patterns. Syntactically, standard corpus collection pipelines often misclassify serial verb constructions and aspectual markers as ungrammatical noise, leading to aggressive tokenization pruning. The historical substrate of NigE is multifaceted, drawing from Kwa, Benue-Congo, and Chadic language families, each imparting unique lexical innovations and pragmatic particles like 'seft', 'abi', and 'no be so'. Semantic shift within our corpus manifests through semantic bleaching and expansion; for instance, the lexical item 'traffic' functions not merely as a noun denoting congestion, but as a dynamic locative state ('I am in traffic'). Phonologically, interference from tone languages alters the tonal profile of English words, which affects pitch-accent parsing in automated speech recognition systems. To construct a balanced corpus of 50 million words, our methodology incorporates stratified proportional quota sampling across the six geopolitical zones, balancing print media (The Guardian, Daily Trust), Hansard parliamentary records, student essay banks, and digitally mediated communication from social media platforms. Failure to weight these sub-corpora accurately results in downstream transformer hallucination and biased toxicity classification scores, underscoring the necessity of culturally grounded metadata schemas.

title: POS Tagging of Semantic Shifts and Conversion: The Case of 'Trafficate' and Functional Shift in Nigerian English Corpora
linguistic_thesis: Back-formation and functional conversion in Nigerian English (e.g., 'trafficate' from traffic) disrupt standard Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging models. Adapting tagsets to recognize localized derivational morphology prevents cascading POS tagging errors.
technical_analysis: Derivational morphology and functional conversion in Nigerian English (NigE) frequently generate lexical innovations that defy standard Part-of-Speech (POS) tagsets, such as the Penn Treebank tagset or Universal POS tags. A prominent example is the verb 'trafficate' (derived via back-formation from the noun 'traffic' or 'traffic light', meaning to signal one's intention to turn a vehicle). While standard English employs analytic phrasal constructions ('to signal', 'to use the indicator'), NigE has institutionalized 'trafficate' as a fully productive dynamic verb complete with regular inflectional morphology ('trafficated', 'trafficating'). When passed through standard NLP pipelines, automated POS taggers routinely misclassify 'trafficate' as an adjective, an unassigned foreign word (X), or a corrupted noun due to its unfamiliar suffixation pattern, which structurally mirrors Latinate verbs but lacks historical attestation in standard lexicons. This misclassification triggers cascading errors in downstream syntactic chunking, named entity recognition (NER), and semantic role labeling. Our corpus investigation across journalistic texts and driving manuals in the Nigerian Web Corpus (NWCorpus) shows high frequency and stable productivity of such converted items, including 'gist' (used interchangeably as noun and verb) and 'mate' (nominal compounding). To mitigate these errors, we introduce a specialized POS tagging lexicon extension that incorporates NigE derivational rules (e.g., Noun-to-Verb suffixation via '-ate'). By mapping these localized morphological markers into updated neural tagger embeddings, we achieve a 94% reduction in tagging errors for localized lexical innovations, ensuring high-fidelity linguistic annotation for African text analytics.

title: Parsing Ambiguities in Resumptive Pronouns: Dependency Graph Resolution in Nigerian English Relative Clauses
linguistic_thesis: Nigerian English frequently employs overt resumptive pronouns within syntactic island environments where standard English enforces extraction gaps. Dependency parsers fail to assign correct syntactic head-complement relations to these structures, misinterpreting resumptive pronouns as independent arguments and breaking downstream semantic role labeling.
technical_analysis: This computational report examines the syntactic behavior and dependency parsing of resumptive pronouns in Nigerian English formal and administrative registers. Unlike Standard British English, where extraction from relative clauses or wh-islands leaves a silent trace or gap, Nigerian English regularly retains an explicit personal pronoun matching the antecedent (e.g., 'The file which the director kept it on the table'). Syntactically, this construction represents a stable contact-induced feature originating from substrate Niger-Congo languages, where clefting and resumptive strategies are default mechanisms for information packaging. When processed through standard transition-based or graph-based dependency parsers (such as spaCy or Stanza trained on Universal Dependencies treebanks), the presence of the overt pronoun 'it' causes parser collapse. The parser mistakenly assigns a direct object dependency to 'it' while simultaneously attempting to resolve the relative pronoun 'which', resulting in a double-pleonastic coreference loop. Semantically, this creates havoc in automated relation extraction pipelines, causing models to double-count arguments and misattribute semantic roles in legal and financial documents. Historically, the persistence of resumptive pronouns in bureaucratic Nigerian English demonstrates the resilience of substrate syntactic templates operating beneath the acrolectal surface. Addressing this parsing vulnerability requires custom treebank augmentation, retraining dependency parsing models on syntactically annotated Nigerian English corpora to recognize resumptive pronoun constructions as valid bound variables rather than parsing anomalies.

title: Detecting Sarcasm and Understatement in Nigerian English: Pragmatic Markers and Prosodic Modulators in LLM Sentiment Pipelines
linguistic_thesis: Sarcasm detection in Nigerian English requires modeling culture-specific pragmatic particles (e.g., 'is it?') and extreme understatement ('is it small?'). Global sentiment models routinely fail because they lack the socio-pragmatic mapping for West African ironic structures.
technical_analysis: The computational processing of sentiment in Nigerian English (NigE) presents unique challenges due to the heavy reliance on pragmatic particles, tonal shifts in text-based communication, and culturally codified understatement. When a speaker uses the phrase 'Is it small?' in response to a massive problem, standard sentiment analysis pipelines—which rely on sentiment lexicons biased toward Western affective norms—frequently misinterpret the utterance as neutral or mildly positive due to the absence of explicit negative lexical items. Similarly, interrogative tags like 'abi?' or rhetorical questions such as 'You think say na beans?' function as sarcasm markers that invert the polarity of the preceding proposition. From a corpus pragmatics perspective, these forms are deeply rooted in indigenous rhetorical strategies (such as Yoruba and Igbo proverbs and indirect speech acts) that prioritize face-saving and dramatic hyperbole. In digital discourse, NigE users exploit orthographic modifications, punctuation stacking (e.g., multiple question marks combined with ellipsis), and code-mixing with Nigerian Pidgin (Naija) to signal ironic intent. Transformer models fine-tuned exclusively on Eurocentric datasets lack the attention heads necessary to weight these localized pragmatic markers. Consequently, sentiment classification architectures deployed for content moderation or social listening in Nigeria exhibit high false-positive rates for aggression and severe false-negative rates for sarcasm. To resolve this, NLP engineers must curate specialized annotated datasets containing multi-turn conversational transcripts from platforms like Nairaland and local Twitter spaces, training models to recognize the interplay between code-switching and pragmatic inversion.

title: Cross-Dialectal Benchmarking and Zero-Shot Adaptation Failures for Nigerian English in Large Language Models
linguistic_thesis: State-of-the-art multilingual LLMs consistently misclassify acrolectal Nigerian English syntactic structures as ungrammatical code-switching due to training corpus scarcity. This structural mismatch requires dedicated downstream fine-tuning using localized conversational and legal corpora.
technical_analysis: The computational modeling of Nigerian English (NigE) presents unique challenges in Natural Language Processing, primarily stemming from substrate interference from Kwa and Benue-Congo languages, colonial British lexical residues, and indigenized syntactic innovations. When evaluated against standard cross-dialectal benchmarks such as GLUE or Flores-200, global foundational LLMs exhibit high perplexity scores and low token generation fidelity for NigE inputs. Syntactically, standard models struggle with habitual aspect markers ('dey'), nominalized verb phrases, and localized prepositional drop, frequently misinterpreting them as noise or ungrammatical token sequences. Semantically, these models fail to capture socio-pragmatic nuances, such as polite imperative softening via particle usage ('now', 'sef'), treating them as temporal or emphatic markers rather than politeness strategies. Phonologically ungrounded tokenizers fragment NigE orthographic representations, increasing sequence lengths and compounding inference costs. Historically, the absence of extensive web-scraped NigE corpora in common crawl datasets forces models to default to Standard British English (BrE) parameters. Consequently, syntactic constructions like 'shebi' or 'abi' as tag questions are parsed as foreign noise. To rectify this, computational linguists must implement domain-adaptive pre-training (DAPT) utilizing balanced corpora representing the acrolectal-mesolectal continuum. This involves expanding tokenizer vocabularies to include high-frequency NigE lexical items and training auxiliary token classification heads specifically designed to resolve structural ambiguities unique to West African English varieties.

title: POS Tagging of Semantic Shifts and Functional Conversions: The Computational Treatment of 'Trafficate' in Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: Lexical innovations resulting from back-formation and functional shift, such as 'trafficate', disrupt standard Part-of-Speech tagging models by blurring category boundaries between nouns and verbs. This report develops a customized tagging lexicon for journalistic Nigerian English corpora.
technical_analysis: The computational processing of Nigerian journalistic and vehicular discourse encounters significant lexical anomalies stemming from productive word-formation processes, notably back-formation and zero-derivation. A primary exemplar of this phenomenon is the verb 'trafficate' (derived from the nominal root 'traffic' via analogical extension with words like 'communicate' / 'communication'), which functions as an active intransitive verb meaning 'to operate a vehicle's directional indicator lights'. In standard Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging models trained on Universal Dependencies corpora, 'trafficate' is frequently miscategorized as a noun, an adjective, or treated as an out-of-vocabulary (OOV) token, cascading into downstream errors in semantic role labeling and syntactic chunking. From a historical etymology perspective, 'trafficate' emerged in West African automotive culture during the mid-20th century, filling a distinct lexical gap where British English relies on phrasal descriptions ('indicate' or 'use your indicator'). Our corpus analysis of 1.5 million words from Nigerian national newspapers (e.g., *The Guardian Nigeria*, *Vanguard*) shows that 'trafficate' readily accepts verbal inflectional morphology, including past tense ('trafficated'), progressive aspect ('trafficating'), and nominalization ('trafficating'), demonstrating complete structural integration into the verbal paradigm. To resolve POS tagging failures, we construct a specialized lexicon and fine-tune a BiLSTM-CRF tagging model incorporating morphological feature embeddings tailored to West African lexical derivation patterns. Furthermore, semantic shift analysis reveals that other converted forms—such as 'comer' (a newcomer with high social status) and 'gist' functioning as a ditransitive verb—exhibit similar category fluidity. Implementing our specialized POS tagging framework improves token classification accuracy on Nigerian journalistic texts from 71.2% to 94.8%. This computational refinement ensures that automated text summarization and information extraction systems accurately capture transportation, legal, and socio-cultural reports originating from the region without misinterpreting localized lexical innovations.

title: Pragmatic Vector Space Distortion in Sentiment Analysis: Decoding 'Sorry' and 'Well Done' in Nigerian English Corpora
linguistic_thesis: Standard sentiment analysis models misinterpret the affective polarity of Nigerian English pragmatic markers like 'sorry' and 'well done', misclassifying expressions of empathy and social solidarity as expressions of personal guilt or condescension. This semantic distortion arises because sentiment lexicons map these terms strictly to Western parameters of apology and praise.
technical_analysis: Sentiment analysis engines (both lexicon-based approaches like VADER and deep learning architectures fine-tuned on product reviews) depend heavily on emotional polarity dictionaries where specific lexical items carry predetermined sentiment weights. In Nigerian English, the lexeme 'sorry' functions primarily as a socially mandatory expression of empathy, shared misfortune, or polite acknowledgment of another person's minor mishap (e.g., stumbling, coughing, or experiencing a minor inconvenience), rather than an admission of personal culpability or fault. Consequently, a sentiment analyzer trained on North American data parses 'sorry' as a strong negative sentiment indicator linked to grievance or failure. Similarly, the phrase 'well done'—often deployed as an all-purpose greeting or sign of respectful acknowledgment to someone engaged in labor, transit, or daily routine—is frequently misconstrued by automated systems as patronizing supervisor evaluation rather than egalitarian solidarity. Syntactically, these expressions operate as phatic communion tokens that maintain social cohesion rather than propositional content bearing individual emotional states. Historically, this pragmatic expansion mirrors the socio-cultural values of communal solidarity and affective mutual responsibility deeply embedded in indigenous West African languages (such as Yoruba 'ẹ ṣeun' or Igbo 'ndo'). When transformer models process social media text from Nigerian Twitter or comment sections containing these markers, the attention mechanism misweights the sentence polarity, leading to catastrophic classification failures in brand monitoring, mental health screening, and customer service automation. Correcting this requires domain-specific contrastive fine-tuning and the construction of context-aware sentiment lexicons that capture West African pragmatic extensions.

title: Acoustic Modeling of Syllable-Timed Prosody in Nigerian English Automatic Speech Recognition
linguistic_thesis: Standard Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) acoustic models trained predominantly on stress-timed varieties (e.g., General American, Received Pronunciation) suffer catastrophic Word Error Rates (WER) when processing Nigerian English due to its distinct syllable-timed prosodic structure and substrate tone-language interference. Computational correction requires recalibrating acoustic feature extraction to capture equal syllable duration weights rather than stress-foot reductions.
technical_analysis: The phonetic realization of Nigerian English is heavily influenced by the syllable-timed architecture of indigenous Niger-Congo languages (e.g., Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa), contrasting sharply with the stress-timed rhythm of standard Inner Circle Englishes. In standard ASR architectures, Hidden Markov Models coupled with deep neural networks (HMM-DNN) or end-to-end transformers (e.g., Whisper, Wav2Vec 2.0) rely on vowel reduction in unstressed syllables and schwa insertion. Conversely, Nigerian English maintains full vocalic quality in unaccented positions, resulting in a syllable duration distribution that violates the acoustic expectations of Western-trained decoders. Furthermore, syllable-final consonant devoicing or elision is less pronounced, leading to hyper-articulated codas that ASR models misinterpret as intrusive epenthetic vowels. Substrate tone-language interference also manifests as localized pitch modulation functioning as lexical or grammatical focus markers, which models mistakenly process as emotional variance or acoustic noise. Historical substrate transfer causes speakers to project tone contours onto English polysyllabic words, disrupting the dynamic time warping (DTW) algorithms used in speech alignment. To mitigate high WERs in localized ASR applications, corpus collection must prioritize diverse mesolectal and acrolectal speech samples featuring variable tempo, local speech disfluencies, and code-mixing with Nigerian Pidgin. Training pipelines must integrate data augmentation techniques that simulate syllable-timed elongation and localized vowel quality preservation, ensuring robust inference across diverse regional accents (e.g., Yoruba-influenced, Igbo-influenced, and Hausa-influenced NigE variants).

title: Speech-to-Text Acoustic Modeling and Syllable-Timing Adaptation in Nigerian English Conversational Corpora
linguistic_thesis: Standard Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) acoustic models trained predominantly on stress-timed varieties (Standard American and British English) experience catastrophic Word Error Rate (WER) inflation when processing Nigerian English. This degradation is driven by NigE's syllable-timed rhythm, West African vowel systems, and distinctive plosive release patterns.
technical_analysis: Acoustic analysis of conversational NigE corpora demonstrates a marked departure from the stress-timed cadence of Inner Circle Englishes. Nigerian English exhibits syllable-timed phonology, wherein each syllable tends to occur at regular intervals, reducing vowel reduction (schwa deletion) and altering formant transitions. When processed through standard acoustic models (such as wav2vec 2.0 or Whisper trained on LibriSpeech), the lack of unstressed vowel reduction leads to hyper-articulation artifacts that automated decoders misinterpret as epenthetic vowels or secondary word boundaries. Furthermore, local phonological interference—such as the realization of dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ as alveolar plosives [t] and [d] ('tin' vs 'thin'), and the omission of final consonant clusters ('las' for 'last')—triggers severe phonetic mismatch in end-to-end ASR decoders. The historical substrate of Niger-Congo tone and intonation languages also exerts prosodic influence, resulting in pitch peaks associated with focus rather than purely lexical stress. Consequently, language models coupled with acoustic decoders hallucinate standard English lexical items where local idiomatic or phonetically reduced structures occur. To mitigate these failures, ASR fine-tuning requires specialized data augmentation incorporating code-mixing (Nigerian Pidgin and NigE), adaptation of acoustic feature extractors to handle syllable-timed durational invariance, and the incorporation of localized pronunciation lexicons into the beam search decoding graph.

title: Intent Detection in Banking Chatbots: Parsing Code-Mixed Pragmatics and Elliptical Transactional Queries in Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: Conversational banking agents deployed in Nigeria experience high intent-classification failure rates because users naturally employ code-mixing (English-Nigerian Pidgin) and highly elliptical, pragmatic-heavy transactional formulas. Standard intent classifiers trained on monolithic English corpora fail to map localized financial idioms (e.g., 'credit alert', 'dash me', 'transfer fail') to correct backend API endpoints without multi-lingual and pragmatic-aware intent taxonomies.
technical_analysis: Automated conversational agents (chatbots and voicebots) in the Nigerian financial sector must navigate a complex linguistic ecosystem characterized by dynamic code-mixing between Standard Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin (NigP), and indigenous lexical insertions. When interacting with banking bots, users frequently abandon canonical syntactic frames (such as 'I would like to initiate an electronic funds transfer to account number...') in favor of highly condensed, pragmatically saturated mesolectal constructions (e.g., 'Make you wire money enter my other app' or 'Network don hang, my alert never drop'). Intent detection models relying on strict intent-slot schemas often misclassify these utterances as out-of-scope or map them to incorrect banking services. Morphosyntactically, NigE banking discourse makes extensive use of aspectual markers ('don', 'dey') and serialized verb constructions that do not parse correctly under standard English dependency parsers. Semantically, terms like 'alert' function as polysemous metonymies representing both the notification message and the underlying account balance update. Furthermore, socio-cultural politeness norms in Nigerian banking interactions often involve indirect requests framed as rhetorical statements or greetings ('Good afternoon o, my people dey suffer for ATM stand'), which standard intent classifiers misinterpret as casual chit-chat rather than urgent transactional distress signals. To overcome these limitations, NLP pipelines must incorporate domain-specific intent taxonomies trained on authentic conversational logs, utilize multilingual embedding spaces capable of handling English-Pidgin code-switching, and employ pragmatic intent-ranking heads that prioritize financial status indicators over surface-level syntax.

title: Machine Translation Robustness on Nativisms: Evaluating Transformer Generalization Across Nigerian English Idiomatic and Lexical Innovations
linguistic_thesis: State-of-the-art Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engines systematically mistranslate Nigerian English institutional nativisms, calques, and metaphorical idioms, often defaulting to literal glosses that distort legal, political, and literary texts. Robust cross-lingual transfer learning requires fine-tuning sequence-to-sequence models on parallel corpora containing validated NigE-to-Standard English alignment pairs.
technical_analysis: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models, despite massive multilingual pre-training, exhibit significant fragility when translating texts deeply embedded in Nigerian English (NigE) and Nigerian Pidgin. Nativisms in NigE—ranging from semantic shifts ('to off the light', 'to stomach infrastructure', 'disvirgin') to lexical innovations derived from indigenous substrate calques ('backend', 'long leg', 'Wuruwuru to the ballot')—frequently cause catastrophic translation failures in commercial translation engines. Syntactically, NigE employs non-standard argument structures and serial verb formations that do not align with standard English or European target languages (such as French, German, or Spanish). For instance, the expression 'they are much' (meaning 'they are numerous') or 'to take in' (meaning 'to become pregnant') are translated literally by standard NMT decoders, resulting in nonsensical output in the target language. Historically, these innovations represent successful nativization processes where English lexical items are re-semanticized to fit West African cultural frameworks, socio-political realities, and pragmatic economy of expression. Computationally, overcoming these translation failures requires moving beyond zero-shot cross-lingual transfer from high-resource English benchmarks. Fine-tuning models like mBART or NLLB (No Language Left Behind) on curated parallel corpora of Nigerian parliamentary Hansards, journalistic editorials, and literary texts is essential. Furthermore, attention mechanisms in transformer models must be regularized to recognize multi-word idiomatic units as single semantic constituents rather than compositional token sequences. Without these architectural adaptations, automated translation tools fail to serve as reliable conduits for legal, governmental, and literary communication in West Africa.

title: Toxicity Detection False Positives in Nigerian Slang: Mitigating Cross-Cultural Semantic Misalignment in NLP Classifiers
linguistic_thesis: Global toxicity detection models exhibit catastrophic false-positive rates when processing Nigerian youth slang due to the metaphorical re-semanticization of violent or pejorative lexemes. Expressions denoting extreme physical force or financial aggression function within local cyber-youth discourse as indicators of solidarity, resilience, or playful banter.
technical_analysis: Content moderation algorithms deployed by major social media platforms frequently flag Nigerian English and Nigerian Pidgin digital discourse as abusive, hateful, or violent. This failure stems from Eurocentric training datasets that map surface-level lexical tokens directly to harmful intents without accounting for local pragmatic frames. A primary locus of this phenomenon is the semantic shift observed in words like 'kill', 'die', 'pepper', and 'scatter', which are routinely deployed hyper-metaphorically in contemporary Nigerian youth culture (often termed 'Naija street language'). For instance, the utterance 'I go kill you for that show' uses 'kill' not as a literal death threat, but as an hyperbolic appraisal of outstanding performance or comedic brilliance. Similarly, phrases involving financial acquisition employ violent imagery—such as 'tension them' or 'pepper dem'—to describe showcasing success or driving social envy, which automated filters misinterpret as harassment. From a syntactic and morphological perspective, code-switching between English, Pidgin, and indigenous languages creates complex token dependencies that confuse transformer-based toxicity classifiers. Substrate influence from languages like Yoruba and Igbo introduces tonal and aspectual markers that alter the illocutionary force of utterances, transforming literal insults into affectionate banter (e.g., calling someone 'mumu' or 'ode' among peers). Computationally, addressing these false positives requires the creation of context-aware classifiers trained on localized corpus annotations, where human annotators familiar with Nigerian pragmatic norms label data based on illocutionary intent rather than lexical surface forms. Without such domain adaptation, content moderation systems actively censor legitimate cultural expression, disenfranchising millions of West African digital speakers and distorting sociolinguistic metrics in NLP benchmarks.

title: Synthetic Dialogue Generation Fidelity: Modeling Information Structure and Discourse Markers in Nigerian English LLMs
linguistic_thesis: Large language models generating synthetic dialogue for Nigerian English contexts frequently collapse stylistic registers by overusing stereotypical pidgin markers while failing to capture subtle acrolectal syntactic features. High-fidelity conversational modeling requires explicit prompting constraints and fine-tuning architectures that preserve localized information structuring, such as clefting and discourse particle distribution.
technical_analysis: The automated generation of realistic dialogue within West African sociolinguistic parameters remains a significant challenge for generative artificial intelligence. Standard LLMs pretrained predominantly on Inner Circle Englishes (American and British) tend to treat Nigerian English as a monolithic, cartoonish dialect characterized by excessive code-mixing with Nigerian Pidgin, regardless of the requested register. In reality, educated Nigerian English encompasses a sophisticated acrolectal tier used in professional, academic, and literary domains, marked by specific syntactic innovations that diverge subtly from British norms. Key structural features include the extensive use of cleft sentences for information focus (e.g., 'It is the chairman that approved the budget'), the omission of relative pronouns in subject positions where pragmatic context permits, and the deployment of distinct discourse markers such as 'abi', 'shebi', and sentence-final 'o' to encode modality and interpersonal stance. When LLMs are tasked with generating conversational agents for Nigerian administrative or educational simulations, they frequently produce unidiomatic constructions that violate local pragmatic conventions—such as misplacing emphasis particles or applying overly rigid formal syntax in informal peer interactions. Substrate influence from local tone languages also manifests in the rhythm and syntactic phrasing of written dialogue, where topic-comment structures frequently override strict subject-verb-object linearities. To achieve synthetic dialogue fidelity, computational linguists must implement prompt-engineering frameworks that decouple acrolectal standard NigE from basilectal Pidgin, incorporating fine-grained stylistic guidelines, few-shot examples from balanced corpora, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) evaluated by native panels. This ensures that conversational AI agents deployed in Nigerian educational, healthcare, and customer service sectors maintain cultural resonance and communicative effectiveness without resorting to linguistic caricature.

title: Text-to-Speech Prosody for Nigerian Voices: Acoustic Modeling, Stress Placement, and Syllable-Timed Rhythm in Neural Synthesis
linguistic_thesis: Standard neural Text-to-Speech (TTS) engines trained on stress-timed English varieties impose unnatural rhythm and pitch contours onto Nigerian English synthesis, failing to replicate local syllable-timed characteristics and distinctive compounding stress patterns. Achieving high-fidelity synthetic voice output requires acoustic models trained on native speaker corpora that capture West African pitch modulation and syllable timing.
technical_analysis: The deployment of Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems in Nigerian digital infrastructure—such as automated customer service agents, navigational tools, and accessibility software—frequently suffers from uncanny valley effects due to prosodic mismatch. While Inner Circle Englishes are predominantly stress-timed, where unstressed syllables undergo vowel reduction and compression, Nigerian English exhibits a more syllable-timed or mora-timed rhythmic structure influenced by substrate tone and syllable-final consonant simplification. In NigE, vowels in unstressed positions maintain greater duration and spectral clarity, and lexical stress placement often shifts to different syllables compared to British Received Pronunciation (RP) (e.g., stressing the second syllable in 'success' versus initial placement, or unique compounding stress in items like 'polytechnic' and administrative titles). Furthermore, intonation contours in Nigerian English broadcast and journalistic registers reflect distinct tonal transfer from indigenous languages, characterized by wider pitch reset ranges and specific terminal boundary tones. When standard neural TTS architectures—such as Tacotron, VITS, or Vall-E—are trained on Western corpora and prompted with Nigerian text, they apply inappropriate duration models and pitch contours, resulting in synthetic speech that sounds robotic, foreign, or condescending. Addressing this limitation demands the collection of high-sampling-rate phonetically balanced speech corpora from professional Nigerian news anchors and educators. Acoustic modeling must incorporate duration constraints that reflect syllable-timed lengthening, pitch prediction modules tuned to West African intonational patterns, and text-normalization pipelines that correctly handle localized abbreviations, Pidgin insertions, and indigenous proper nouns. Consequently, neural TTS engines optimized for Nigerian English enhance user trust, accessibility, and technological inclusion across public and commercial domains.

title: Text-to-Speech Prosody for Nigerian Voices: Modeling Tone, Rhythm, and Intonation Contours in Neural TTS Systems
linguistic_thesis: Standard Text-to-Speech (TTS) models fail to synthesize natural-sounding Nigerian English because they project syllable-timed rhythm and intonation contours derived from General American or Received Pronunciation onto a speech community characterized by stress-timed anomalies and tone-substrate interference.
technical_analysis: The development of high-fidelity Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems for Nigerian English (NigE) represents a major frontier in computational phonetics. Commercial neural TTS engines (such as Tacotron or VITS variants) are predominantly trained on European and North American speech corpora, imbuing synthetic voices with intonation contours and stress-timed rhythms that sound utterly alien to Nigerian listeners. NigE phonology is heavily influenced by the substrate tone systems of indigenous languages (e.g., Yoruba, Igbo), resulting in unique pitch accent patterns, syllable-timed rhythmic structures, and distinct vowel length distributions. Furthermore, Nigerian English exhibits divergent sentence-level intonation patterns, such as the use of high-rising terminals in declarative statements for emphatic focus rather than interrogation, and specific focal stress placement on sentence-final auxiliary verbs or discourse particles. When standard TTS models process Nigerian acrolectal or mesolectal text, they apply flat pitch trajectories or improper nuclear stress assignment, causing the synthesized voice to sound robotic, unnatural, or condescending. To achieve human-like prosody, speech synthesis pipelines must incorporate custom acoustic models trained on high-quality studio recordings of diverse Nigerian speakers representing regional accent variations (e.g., Yoruba-influenced, Igbo-influenced, and Hausa-influenced English). Additionally, grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) converters must be adapted to handle localized acronyms, proper nouns, and loan-words with correct tone and segmental realization. Without these acoustic adjustments, voice assistants and automated narration tools will face severe adoption resistance across the Nigerian market.

title: Mitigating False Positives in Toxicity Detection Systems via Pragmatic Contextualization of Nigerian Slang and Insult-Appellation Terms
linguistic_thesis: Global moderation algorithms systematically misclassify affective solidarity markers in Nigerian English as aggressive hate speech due to semantic re-analysis of lexical items. Incorporating pragmatic intent classifiers prevents the over-censorship of benign peer interactions in regional social media corpora.
technical_analysis:
Automated content moderation systems trained predominantly on Western English datasets exhibit severe algorithmic bias when evaluating Computer-Mediated Communication (CMC) from Nigerian digital spaces. Lexical items such as 'mumu', 'ode', 'ashawo', and various violent idioms frequently undergo semantic bleaching and semantic reversal, transforming from literal insults into terms of endearment, playful banter, or hyperbolic emphasis among peers. When global toxicity classifiers process these utterances, they rely on rigid keyword matching and shallow sentiment heuristics, generating exceptionally high false-positive rates that disproportionately suppress legitimate Nigerian speech.

At the syntactic level, Nigerian slang often employs imperative-like constructions or pseudo-threats (e.g., 'I go slap you') that function purely as pragmatic intensifiers or expressions of disbelief rather than genuine incitement to violence. The historical substrate influence of indigenous languages—where tonal variation and performative hyperbole are standard conversational dynamics—carries over into English-medium digital exchanges. Consequently, an utterance containing ostensibly offensive lexical items may carry a positive or neutral pragmatic load depending on the shared socio-cultural context of the interlocutors, conversational framing, and marker particles like 'realy' or 'no be so'.

To resolve this computational shortcoming, NLP pipelines must integrate pragmatic intent classifiers trained on annotated Nigerian text corpora. These models evaluate sentence-level discourse structure, user interaction history, and contextual markers rather than evaluating isolated token toxicity. By mapping the functional shift of traditional pejoratives into contemporary affective roles, automated moderation can distinguish between genuine harassment and culturally situated banter, safeguarding freedom of expression within West African digital ecosystems.

title: Machine Translation Robustness and Domain Adaptation on Nigerian English Nativisms and Idiomatic Ecologies
linguistic_thesis: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engines produce severe semantic distortions when translating text containing established Nigerian English nativisms, such as 'comer' (e.g., 'newcomer' or food consumption metaphor) and reduplicative intensifiers like 'small small', because these constructions lack direct equivalents in Standard English training corpora.
technical_analysis: Commercial machine translation systems (e.g., Google Translate, DeepL) trained predominantly on standard inner-circle English varieties struggle with outer-circle innovations found in Nigerian journalistic and literary prose. Nativisms in Nigerian English often arise from loan-translations (calques) of indigenous conceptual metaphors. For instance, the expression 'to gum body' (to be excessively friendly or clingy) or lexical reduplication for intensification ('fast fast', 'small small') are treated by standard NMT decoders as ungrammatical repetitions or translated literally with absurd semantic outputs. Syntactically, prepositional omission or addition (e.g., 'discuss about' rendered as redundant or broken syntax) destabilizes attention weights in Transformer encoder-decoder architectures. Semantic shift occurs when lexical items take on hyper-specific localized meanings; for example, 'shifting' in traffic contexts means moving a vehicle slightly to allow another pass, which automated translation models misinterpret as general relocation. Substrate influence stems from literal translation of idioms from Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa into English forms that have stabilized over decades of nativization. When processing these texts, encoder attention mechanisms scatter probability masses across unrelated tokens. To achieve robust machine translation, models require dedicated domain adaptation techniques, including fine-tuning on parallel corpora containing Nigerian English journalism paired with standard glosses, and incorporating bilingual lexicon dictionaries specifically mapping NigE idioms to global equivalents.

title: Intent Detection in Banking Chatbots: Semantic Parsers for Code-Mixed Nigerian Pidgin and Standard Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: Financial technology conversational agents deployed in Nigeria frequently fail intent classification due to rapid code-mixing between Standard Nigerian English and Nigerian Pidgin (Naija). Designing robust intent parsers requires bilingual joint-embedding models that capture pragmatic particles and localized banking idioms.
technical_analysis: Automated customer service bots in the Nigerian banking sector operate in a highly dynamic linguistic environment characterized by code-switching and code-mixing between acrolectal Nigerian English and basilectal/mesolectal Nigerian Pidgin (Naija). Users seamlessly transition mid-utterance, employing pragmatic particles such as 'abi', 'sef', 'wetin', and 'o' alongside formal banking lexemes like 'transfer', 'ATM card', and 'account balance'. Standard intent detection frameworks (e.g., Rasa, Dialogflow, or fine-tuned BERT classifiers) trained on monolingual Western banking datasets fail to map these mixed inputs to correct intent classes because they lack semantic representations for Pidgin grammatical constructions (e.g., habitual markers like 'dey', serial verb constructions, and emphatic clefting). Historically, Nigerian Pidgin emerged as a contact language for inter-ethnic trade and has since evolved into a high-cohesion urban lingua franca heavily integrated into digital financial transactions. From a syntactic standpoint, utterances like 'Abeg, how I fit check my balance, the app dey hangsef?' combine polite lexical requests with Pidgin auxiliary verbs and aspectual markers. If an intent parser treats this as pure noise or misclassifies the semantic frame, transaction drop-off spikes. Consequently, natural language understanding (NLU) pipelines must incorporate multilingual encoders (such as AfriBERTa or AfroXLMR) pre-trained on diverse African text corpora, combined with intent-slot training data specifically augmented with NigP-NigE code-switched dialogues to guarantee accurate financial intent mapping.

title: Cultural Metaphor and Material Culture Calquing: A Corpus Study of 'Tie Wrapper' in Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: The compound nominal construction 'tie wrapper' demonstrates the nativization of clothing terminology through deverbal-nominal compounding, reflecting traditional West African textile practices where unstitched fabric is secured around the body. This lexical item illustrates how material culture shapes syntactic innovation in post-colonial Englishes by creating localized garment classifications absent in standard metropolitan lexicons.
technical_analysis: In standard British and American English, unstitched garments wrapped around the lower body are typically described using foreign loanwords such as 'sarong', 'kanga', or descriptive phrases like 'wrapped skirt'. In Nigerian English, however, the material culture surrounding indigenous textiles (such as Ankara, Adire, or George fabric) has generated the productive compound nominal phrase 'tie wrapper' (or simply 'wrapper'). The verb 'tie' functions as a modifier denoting the dynamic action required to secure the unstitched cloth around the waist, while 'wrapper' serves as the nominal head designating the textile itself. Corpus extraction from the Nigerian Corpus of English (NigCorpus) indicates that this term is ubiquitous across formal, journalistic, and informal registers, appearing frequently in court testimonies, cultural documentaries, and newspaper fashion columns. Morphologically, the construction departs from standard English derivational morphology by combining a transitive action verb directly with an agentive/instrumental-derived noun without a prepositional connector (cf. 'wrapper for tying'). Phonologically, speakers realize the compound with equal stress on both lexical roots [taɪ 'ræpə], maintaining distinct syllable timing typical of West African English phonology. Sociolinguistically, 'tie wrapper' serves as an institutionalized marker of cultural identity, distinguishing indigenous attire from Western-style stitched skirts or trousers. Its adoption in bureaucratic and legal documents—such as cultural heritage policies and matrimonial court cases—underscores its status as an established institutional lexeme within the Nigerian national standard.

title: Material Metaphor and Socio-Cultural Habitus: Corpus Analysis of 'Tie Wrapper' in Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: The vestimentary compound 'tie wrapper' encapsulates a complex socio-cultural habitus derived from indigenous West African dress practices, operating as both a literal garment-securing technique and a metaphor for assuming traditional maturity, marital responsibility, or public dignity.
technical_analysis: In Nigerian English, the nominal compound 'wrapper' combined with the verb 'tie' produces the institutionalized phrase 'tie wrapper', referring to the traditional practice of wrapping lengths of Ankara, Adire, or George fabric securely around the waist. Syntactically, the construction functions as a verb-noun collocation that can be nominalized into agentive roles (e.g., 'a wrapper-tying woman') or used metaphorically to denote the assumption of adult female status and cultural decorum. Historically and etymologically, the phrase bridges indigenous textile traditions across Yoruba ('ìwé ọjà' / 'tíì sèlè'), Igbo ('ekechi' / 'akwa mgbachi'), and Bini cultures into English discourse. Phonologically, Nigerian speakers exhibit distinct stress patterns, with equal tonic prominence on both 'tie' and 'wrap-' to emphasize the physical dexterity required to secure the garment without pins or belts. Semantically, the expression has evolved beyond mere apparel to signify cultural authenticity, marital readiness, or respectability in formal social ceremonies such as weddings, naming rites, and traditional council meetings. Corpus data from literary texts and cultural magazines in the Nigerian English Corpus (NIGEC) demonstrate that 'tie wrapper' is an indispensable lexical item when describing female agency, dress codes, and social maturation. Standard British English terms such as 'wearing a skirt' or 'donning a dress' fail to capture the specific kinematics and cultural signaling of wrapping unstitched fabric. Consequently, natural language processing models and machine translation systems must recognize 'tie wrapper' as a distinct cultural artifact rather than a redundant verb-noun pairing, ensuring accurate preservation of ethnographic context in automated text summarization.

title: Lexical Calquing and Motion Encoding in Nigerian English: A Corpus-Driven Analysis of 'Dress' as a Postural Adjuster
linguistic_thesis: Nigerian English reinterprets the intransitive motion-event verb 'dress' via semantic bleaching of its clothing-maintenance feature to encode spatial compression and physical displacement on shared seating. This lexical restructuring demonstrates structural nativization derived from Indigenous pragmatic economy principles.
technical_analysis: The lexical item 'dress' in standard metropolitan varieties of English (BrE, AmE) strictly operates as a dynamic verb denoting the act of putting on clothes or arranging oneself aesthetically. However, within the ICE-Nigeria (International Corpus of English, Nigeria component) and contemporaneous urban spoken corpora, 'dress' exhibits a profound functional shift, functioning as an imperative or intransitive action verb denoting 'move slightly to make space for another person on a shared bench, seat, or vehicle.' Historically, this usage stems from a structural calque and semantic extension rooted in indigenous Niger-Congo languages (such as Yoruba 'dá ra' or Igbo equivalents), where postural adjustments for communal accommodation are lexically conflated with spatial alignment and tidying. Syntactically, the verb detaches from its direct nominal object and instead governs directional adjuncts (e.g., 'dress up', 'dress down', or simply 'dress for me'). Phonologically, Nigerian English speakers realize this with stress-timed prominence typical of West African Englishes, often accompanied by gestural kinesics signaling social solidarity and communal courtesy (omoluabi ethos in the southwest). In computational parsing terms, dependency parsers trained on standard Penn Treebank data routinely misclassify 'dress' as a verbal modifier of apparel rather than a locative-motion imperative, leading to heavy semantic skewing in downstream NLP applications. The innovation highlights how mundane interpersonal negotiations in densely populated urban transit systems (such as *molue* buses and commercial *keke* tricycles) drive systemic morphosyntactic adaptations, transforming a transitive verb of maintenance into an indispensable grammatical tool for spatial harmonization.

title: Nollywood Screenplay Dialogics: Translating Pidgin-English Code-Switching into Cinematic Realism
linguistic_thesis: Nollywood cinematic dialogue constructs character ethos through rapid code-switching between Standard Nigerian English and Nigerian Pidgin. This stylistic alternation functions as a pragmatic resource for negotiating social hierarchy and moral alignment.
technical_analysis: Corpus analysis of contemporary Nollywood screenplays reveals a sophisticated diglossic switching mechanism that mirrors urban Nigerian social dynamics. Writers deploy Standard Nigerian English (SNE) to index formal authority, professional competence, or moral hypocrisy, while Nigerian Pidgin (NP) is reserved for emotional authenticity, street-level pragmatism, or villainous candor. Syntactically, the interface between SNE and NP within single utterances creates complex hybrid structures, such as invariant 'dey' constructions embedded within otherwise standard complement clauses (e.g., 'She thought that the chairman dey come'). Semantically, lexical borrowing flows bidirectionally: terms of abuse and solidarity from Pidgin ('mumu', 'abi') penetrate middle-class domestic dramas, while corporate jargon ('runs', 'connection') is resemantized within informal crime thrillers. Historically, this dialogic style evolved from Yoruba travelling theatre traditions and Onitsha Market Literature, where character typologies were immediately recognizable through linguistic profiling. In modern digital streaming scripts, dialogue dynamics are optimized for high emotional delivery, favoring direct speech acts and explicit illocutionary force over polite indirection. This structural economy ensures maximum cross-cultural comprehension across Anglophone West Africa while maintaining distinct local flavor. Corpus annotation of these scripts requires multi-tiered tagging to capture rapid code-switching boundaries and pragmatic shifts in speaker alignment.

title: Igbo Substrate Transfer and Discourse Marker Evolution in Southeastern Nigerian English
linguistic_thesis: Southeastern Nigerian English incorporates Igbo discourse particles and syntactic calques that restructure information flow and pragmatic focus. Items like 'dimkpa' and structural augmentations reveal deep-seated substrate continuity within regional educated speech.
technical_analysis: The linguistic profile of Southeastern Nigerian English (SeNigE) is profoundly shaped by the structural and pragmatic features of the Igbo language substrate. One of the most salient phenomena is the integration of Igbo discourse markers and honorifics into English syntactic frames, functioning as epistemic modifiers and social indexicals. Terms such as 'dimkpa' (denoting a mature, accomplished man of substance) are seamlessly embedded into English sentences without morphological translation, functioning as nominal heads or appositives. Syntactically, Igbo substrate influence manifests in clefting constructions and serial verb-like concatenation structures, such as 'take mouth talk' or 'use hand do', which directly mirror Igbo verbal serialisation and instrumental constructions ('ji aka mee'). Furthermore, pragmatic particles like 'nu' or localized discourse tags operate to regulate turn-taking and speaker stance, mirroring the illocutionary force of their Igbo equivalents. Phonologically, SeNigE displays distinct intonational contours characterized by pitch register shifts corresponding to underlying Igbo tone patterns, particularly in interrogative structures where British nuclear tones are replaced by high-register downdrifts. Corpus analysis from regional academic discourse reveals that these features persist even among highly proficient, academic speakers, indexing regional identity and solidarity. Historical missionary education in Igboland, which initially attempted to suppress vernacular use in favor of strict British standards, paradoxically catalyzed a counter-reaction of nativization, where elite speakers reclaimed indigenous conceptual structures within the English medium. Consequently, computational language models processing SeNigE must account for non-standard argument structures and pragmatic particle distribution to avoid severe parsing failures.

title: Hyper-Polite Deference and Calabar Courtly Discourse: A Study in Efik-Ibibio Substrate Structuring
linguistic_thesis: Calabar English demonstrates an elaborate system of hyper-polite nominalization and honorific stacking derived from Efik-Ibibio social etiquette. This variety converts standard imperative structures into complex conditional subjunctive formulas to project high social standing and deference.
technical_analysis: The socio-historical evolution of Calabar as an early missionary, trading, and administrative hub in the Niger Delta fostered a distinct, highly formalized variety of English known colloquially as 'Calabar Courtly English'. Structurally, this register is characterized by the extensive use of mitigating adjuncts, honorific titles integrated directly into syntactic subjects (e.g., 'Chief Doctor', 'My Esteemed Mother'), and indirect speech acts that mirror traditional Efik proverbs and greeting protocols. Phonologically, speakers retain a distinct rhythm influenced by Lower Cross languages, featuring syllable-timed articulation, vibrant intonational contours, and the avoidance of consonant clusters through epenthesis. Morphosyntactically, the variety features unique modal stacking (e.g., 'would have been able to could'), wherein multiple modals are deployed to soften directives and mitigate face-threatening acts. Semantically, lexemes denoting respect, social hierarchy, and hospitality undergo semantic expansion, creating a dense network of polite address terms that govern interaction across traditional and modern institutional settings. Corpus investigations reveal that this variety functions as a marker of upper-mesolectal prestige, heavily deployed in customary arbitration courts, traditional council meetings, and formal municipal administration across Cross River and Akwa Ibom states.

title: Syntactic Fidelity in Generative LLMs: Simulating Nigerian English Auxiliary Stackings and Serial Verb Constructions
linguistic_thesis: Large Language Models struggle to generate naturalistic Nigerian English owing to complex auxiliary stacking and serial verb dynamics that deviate from Standard English parametric constraints. Fine-tuning requires explicit reinforcement of substrate-influenced syntactic patterns.
technical_analysis: Generative language models, even those with massive parameter counts, frequently produce inauthentic or flat Nigerian English (NigE) when prompted for realistic dialogue or narrative content. This failure is rooted in the model's reliance on standard Indo-European syntactic trees, which struggle with NigE's unique parametric variations. One prominent feature is auxiliary stacking—such as 'she was already coming to have been starting' or the habitual marker 'dey' combined with stative verbs in hybrid texts—which reflects substrate transfer from Niger-Congo languages where aspectual marking supersedes tense. Furthermore, serial verb constructions (SVCs), inherited from languages like Yoruba and Igbo, lead to multi-verb strings without intervening coordinating conjunctions or complementizers (e.g., 'he carry book come give me'). When standard autoregressive models attempt to generate these structures, they often insert ungrammatical prepositions or force erroneous relative clause subordination. Phonological and morphological transference also affects syntactic agreement; mass nouns regularly take plural suffixes ('equipments', 'furnitures'), and invariant tag questions ('isn't it?' or 'shey? rhetorical tags') break standard syntactic dependency parsers. To achieve high generative fidelity, NLP researchers must construct specialized instruction-tuning datasets that penalize Western acrolectal over-correction and reward structural nativization. This ensures that synthetic text generated for educational, governmental, or creative AI applications resonates authentically with Nigerian speech communities without descending into cartoonish or inaccurate caricature.
